h1: How Much Does a Photo Booth Rental Cost in NYC?
excerpt: There's no single sticker price for a photo booth in NYC — here's what actually moves the number, so you know what you're paying for before you ask for a quote.

heroImg.alt: Photo booth set up at an event in New York City

body.heading: Why there's no flat rate
paragraphs: Ask five photo booth companies what a rental costs and you'll get five different answers, and honestly, ours would be five different answers too depending on your event. That's not evasiveness — it's because a photo booth quote is built from several moving parts, not read off a single price list. The booth type you pick, how many hours you need it running, how far it has to travel, and which add-ons you want all move the number independently.

That said, you shouldn't have to fill out a form just to get a sense of scale. Our Studio Booth, one of our most-booked options, starts at $899 for 3 hours. That's a real starting point, not a teaser rate — custom packages (longer rentals, premium booths, branded activations) are priced to the event itself, which is why we don't post a single ceiling number. What follows is what actually moves the price up or down from that starting point, so a quote makes sense the moment it lands in your inbox.

body.heading: Booth type is the biggest factor
paragraphs: The booth itself is usually the largest single driver of price. A full-length mirror booth with an animated touchscreen and studio lighting is a different piece of equipment — and a different install — than a roaming photo booth, where an attendant simply walks the room with a handheld capture system and there's no structure to set up at all. A branded booth built around a custom wrap, start screen and campaign overlays carries more production than a standard rental, and something like a mosaic wall, where every guest photo prints as a sticker that builds into one giant image, is its own category of setup and output entirely.

None of these are "better" or "worse" — they're suited to different rooms and different goals. That's why the fastest way to a realistic number is telling us what the event actually is; we'll recommend a booth to fit it rather than starting from a price and working backward.

body.heading: Hours, and what happens outside them
paragraphs: How long you book the booth for is the second-biggest lever, and most events don't need it running all night — three to four hours is typical for a wedding reception, and it's usually better spent live during the highest-energy stretch than sitting idle earlier in the evening. If your event runs long and you want the booth to keep going, additional hours beyond what you booked are $125 per hour.

One thing worth knowing up front: our team arrives about an hour before your scheduled start time to set up and test everything. If you need us on site earlier than that — for early venue access or extra setup time — an idle fee of $150 per hour applies. It's not a penalty, it's just the honest cost of an attendant standing by rather than driving to another booking.

body.heading: Travel and your borough
paragraphs: We're based in Brooklyn and serve Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens, the Bronx, Staten Island, Long Island, Westchester, New Jersey and Connecticut. Travel is quoted from your venue's ZIP code before you book, so it's part of your upfront number rather than a surprise on the invoice — a Williamsburg wedding and a Westchester one simply won't carry the same travel line, and we'll tell you which up front.

body.heading: Add-ons that change the number
paragraphs: Custom print templates built around your names, date or logo are standard on most bookings. Beyond that, things like a flower wall or champagne wall as a backdrop, branded overlays and a microsite for a corporate activation, or an extra roaming attendant to cover seated tables at a large wedding all add to the quote — and all are optional, so you're never paying for something you didn't ask for.

Every rental, regardless of booth or add-ons, includes a trained on-site attendant, unlimited prints for your guests, and our $3 million liability policy with a same-day certificate of insurance if your venue needs one. Those aren't upsells — they're built into every quote we send.

Because pricing is genuinely specific to your date, venue and booth choice, the fastest way to a real number is our quote form — it takes about 30 seconds and comes back with pricing built for your actual event, travel included.

faqs.a: Our Studio Booth starts at $899 for 3 hours — that's the most reliable anchor point we can give without a form. From there, price moves based on which booth you choose, how many hours you need, and where your venue is. Custom and premium packages are priced to the event itself, so the fastest way to a real number for anything beyond the starting rate is our quote form, which takes about 30 seconds.

faqs.a: A trained on-site attendant, unlimited prints for your guests during your rental, and our $3 million liability policy with a same-day certificate of insurance if your venue requires one. Travel is calculated from your venue's ZIP code and included in the quote up front, not added later.

faqs.a: Additional hours beyond what you booked are $125 per hour, arranged on the day if the party's still going. If you need our team on site earlier than the standard hour-before arrival for setup, that's an idle fee of $150 per hour.

meta.title: Corporate Photo Booth Ideas | Magic Mirror Brooklyn
meta.description: Photo booth ideas for corporate events that go beyond a generic backdrop — branding, lead capture and the right booth for launches, parties and trade shows.

h1: Corporate Event Photo Booth Ideas That Actually Get Used
excerpt: The difference between a corporate photo booth people actually line up for and one that sits empty in the corner usually comes down to a handful of decisions made before the event.

heroImg.alt: Branded photo booth activation at a corporate event in New York

body.heading: Start with what the event needs to do
paragraphs: A photo booth does a different job depending on who the event is for. At an internal event — a holiday party, a summer outing, an awards night — it gives coworkers who don't otherwise talk a reason to stand together, and everyone leaves with something to take home. At an external event — a product launch, a trade show stand, a brand activation — the booth becomes a marketing channel. Every photo that leaves carries your branding out to an audience the attendee already trusts, which is distribution you can't buy directly.
Deciding which of those two jobs your event needs first changes almost every choice that follows, from which booth to book to how much lead time to plan for.

body.heading: Branding the whole experience, not just the backdrop
paragraphs: A branded photo booth can be wrapped entirely in your colors, with a custom start screen, branded photo overlays, custom-printed backdrops, and a hosted online gallery or microsite for the images. The reason this matters more at a corporate event than a private one: a generic booth sitting in the middle of a carefully branded activation undermines the rest of the spend. Consistency is the actual product.

Lead time matters here. A full physical wrap needs two to three weeks' notice so graphics can be printed and applied correctly. If your date is closer than that, digital-only branding — the start screen, overlays and gallery — turns around considerably faster and still carries the brand through every photo.

body.heading: Make it collect something, not just photos
paragraphs: Surveys and short questionnaires can be built directly into the booth flow, so you're gathering product feedback at the exact moment attendees are engaged rather than emailing them a week later when the event has left their mind. Opt-in contact capture builds a compliant list for remarketing, and you receive a report of what was collected — the images and any data captured belong to you, not us.

That turns the booth into an activation you can put numbers against afterward: engagement volume, opt-in rate, shares. That's a very different conversation with a marketing lead than "people seemed to like it."

body.heading: Picking the right booth for the room
paragraphs: For a multi-day trade show or a conference floor where footfall is spread across a full day rather than concentrated into one evening, a roaming photo booth usually outperforms a static one — an attendant works the aisle with a handheld capture system instead of waiting for a line to form at a fixed booth. For an internal celebration where you want one big collective moment, a mosaic wall is worth considering: every guest's photo prints as a sticker they place themselves, and by the end of the night the wall has built into one large image, often a company logo. For a launch or sponsored activation where the branding has to be airtight, the branded booth — full wrap, custom start screen, overlays and microsite — is built for exactly that.

body.heading: Handling the venue logistics
paragraphs: Midtown offices, hotel ballrooms, convention centers and gallery spaces all come with their own loading dock windows, freight elevator bookings, building engineers and certificate-of-insurance requirements. We handle that coordination as a matter of course, planning load-in around your venue's actual access rather than the floor plan on paper — and we carry a $3 million policy, so the COI paperwork is rarely the thing holding up approval.

faqs.a: Yes, we work with corporate clients regularly. For established accounts we can also arrange payment terms — an opening order of $5,000 or more is required to set an account up.

faqs.a: Two to three weeks for a physical wrap, since graphics have to be printed and applied. Digital branding — the start screen, overlays and gallery — can be produced much faster if your date is closer than that.

faqs.a: Yes. Images and any opt-in contact data gathered at your activation belong to you. We provide the gallery and the report, and you decide what happens with it next.

faqs.a: For a multi-day show with footfall spread across the day, the roaming photo booth usually covers more ground than a static booth, since an attendant brings the camera to people rather than waiting for a line.

meta.title: How to Choose a Wedding Photo Booth | Magic Mirror Brooklyn
meta.description: Which photo booth suits a wedding, when to run it during your reception, and what your NYC venue will need — a practical guide for couples planning theirs.

h1: How to Choose a Wedding Photo Booth in NYC
excerpt: The right wedding photo booth depends less on which one looks nicest online and more on your guest list, your venue, and when you run it — here's how to think it through.

heroImg.alt: Bride and groom posing at the wedding photo booth in New York City

body.heading: Why a photo booth earns its place at a wedding
paragraphs: Your photographer captures the day. A photo booth captures what your guests did with it — the table of cousins who piled in six at a time, the uncle who found the boa, the friends who came back four times over the night. Those are different photographs, and you generally only get them if there's a booth in the room.

There's a practical argument too. A booth keeps the room busy during the flat spots — the gap between dinner and dancing, the stretch while the band changes over — and gives guests who aren't dancing somewhere to be. Couples routinely tell us their guests stayed later than expected, and the booth is usually part of why.

body.heading: When to run it during your reception
paragraphs: Most weddings book three to four hours of booth time. The sweet spot is opening as cocktail hour ends and running through the heart of the dance floor, so the booth is live while the energy is highest rather than sitting idle through dinner speeches.

If your reception runs long, it's usually better to start the booth later than to start it early and have it close before the night peaks. Talk this through with your booth company when you get a quote, rather than just defaulting to more hours than you need.

body.heading: Matching the booth to your wedding
paragraphs: The mirror booth is the most-booked choice for weddings, largely because the full-length format handles whole wedding parties at once and works for every generation in the room, from the flower girl to the grandparents. The glam booth suits black-tie weddings where you want the photos to look as considered as the outfits — a black-and-white, skin-smoothing look closer to a red-carpet shot than a snapshot. The 360 booth, where a slow-motion camera orbits your guests on a lit platform, has become the pick for younger, more shareable crowds.

For guest lists over about 150, it's worth pairing a static booth with a roaming attendant so the seated tables get covered too, rather than everyone funneling into one queue at the same booth all night.

body.heading: What your venue will need from you
paragraphs: Most NYC wedding venues ask for a certificate of insurance naming them as additionally insured before they'll confirm your vendor. A $3 million policy with same-day COI turnaround is worth confirming with any booth company you're considering — it's one less thing to chase in the weeks before the wedding.

On the setup side, plan for the booth to arrive about an hour before your start time and take roughly 20 minutes to set up. A 10ft x 10ft footprint is ideal, 8ft x 8ft is the minimum, and it needs a standard outlet within 15 feet that isn't already shared with the DJ or catering. Flagging this with your venue coordinator early avoids a last-minute scramble for power.

faqs.q: How many hours should we book for a wedding?
faqs.a: Three to four hours covers most receptions. Rather than sell you an extra hour you don't need, we'd rather help you place those hours well — tell us your run sheet and we'll suggest a start time.

faqs.q: Can the booth match our wedding colors?
faqs.a: Yes. The print template is designed around your names, date and palette, and you choose the backdrop from our range. A flower wall is also available if you want the backdrop to be part of the decor rather than just behind it.

faqs.q: Which booth do most couples book?
faqs.a: The mirror booth is our most-booked wedding option because its full-length format works for entire wedding parties and every age in the room. The glam booth suits black-tie weddings, and the 360 booth tends to draw younger, more shareable crowds.

faqs.q: Do we get all the photos afterward?
faqs.a: Yes. Every image from the night lands in an online gallery you can download in full and share with guests, on top of the unlimited prints handed out at the reception.

faqs.q: How much space and power does the booth need?
faqs.a: A 10ft x 10ft space is ideal, 8ft x 8ft is the minimum, plus a standard outlet within 15 feet that isn't shared with the DJ or catering. We'll confirm this against your specific venue before the day.

faqs.a: Yes. We carry a $3 million liability policy, and if your venue needs a certificate of insurance naming them as additionally insured, we turn it around the same day you send their contact details.

meta.title: Photo Booth Space Requirements NYC | Magic Mirror Brooklyn
meta.description: How much floor space, ceiling height and power a photo booth needs at your NYC venue, broken down by booth type, so you can confirm the fit before you book.

h1: Photo Booth Space Requirements for Any NYC Venue
excerpt: Every booth we bring needs some combination of floor space, ceiling clearance and a nearby outlet — here's exactly how much, by booth type, so your venue coordinator isn't guessing.

heroImg.alt: Mirror photo booth set up with room to spare at an NYC event venue

body.heading: Why we ask about your venue before the day of
paragraphs: Nearly every setup problem we've ever run into traces back to the same thing: nobody confirmed the space until the truck was already outside. A booth that looks compact in a showroom photo still needs a real footprint, a real ceiling height and a real outlet, and venues vary enormously — a hotel ballroom and a brownstone parlor floor are not the same planning problem.

So before your event, we ask for the room, and ideally a photo, so we can tell you honestly whether your first-choice booth fits or whether something else in our range is the better call. What follows is the actual math we use.

body.heading: The standard footprint: mirror, glam, AI and GIF booths
paragraphs: Most of our open-air booths — the magic mirror, the glam booth, the AI booth and the GIF booth — share the same baseline: 10ft x 10ft is the ideal footprint, giving room for the booth itself, a backdrop, a props table and a red carpet if you want one. When a venue is tighter than that, we can compress down to a minimum of 8ft x 8ft with 7.5ft of ceiling clearance, which still fits the full experience, just without the extra breathing room.

Every one of these booths needs a standard 110V, 5-amp, 3-prong outlet within 15 feet of the setup spot, ideally one that isn't already shared with the DJ's rig or a chafing dish warmer — a shared circuit is one of the more common causes of a mid-event trip.

body.heading: Booths that need more room: 360, vogue and the Glambot
paragraphs: A few of our booths need more than the standard footprint because of how they operate. The 360 booth's camera arm sweeps a full circle around guests standing on a platform, and a crowd reliably gathers to watch — 8ft x 8ft with 7.5ft of clearance is the floor, but 12ft x 12ft is genuinely better if the room allows it, since the queue becomes part of the show rather than blocking a walkway. It also needs a dedicated 15 or 20-amp outlet, not a standard one.

The vogue booth and the Glambot's robotic arm both want a similar footprint — around 12ft x 12ft with clear ceiling height — plus their own dedicated outlet. Because both are larger installs than a standard booth, load-in at a venue with restricted access can take closer to two hours rather than the usual twenty minutes, so we plan that time in ahead of the day rather than discovering it on arrival.

body.heading: Tight venues, brownstones and outdoor setups
paragraphs: Some of our most-requested venues are also our tightest. A Park Slope or Crown Heights parlor floor often means a narrow stairwell, which changes what we bring — a compact mirror booth or a roaming attendant travels light and fits where a full 360 rig wouldn't, and we confirm a shared brownstone electrical panel's capacity before the day rather than during it.

Outdoor setups follow a different checklist entirely: a level, dry surface, cover from direct weather, and the same outlet requirement as indoors. We'll walk through your specific outdoor site with you in advance rather than assuming a backyard works the same way a tent does.

body.heading: What to send us before you book
paragraphs: The room name (or a photo of it), the rough dimensions if you have them, and whether there's an elevator, stairs or a loading dock involved is usually all we need to confirm your booth choice fits. We arrive about an hour before your scheduled start time to set up and test everything, and setup itself typically takes around 20 minutes once we're in the room.

If your venue needs us on-site earlier than that — for early access or extra setup time at a tighter space — an idle fee of $150 per hour applies. It's not a penalty, just the honest cost of an attendant standing by rather than driving to another booking.

faqs.q: How much space does a standard photo booth need?
faqs.a: 10ft x 10ft is the ideal footprint for our mirror, glam, AI and GIF booths, and we can compress to a minimum of 8ft x 8ft with 7.5ft of ceiling clearance when a venue is tight. We'll confirm the exact fit against your venue before you book.

faqs.q: What if my venue is smaller than that?
faqs.a: Tell us the room and we'll recommend a booth that actually fits — a compact mirror booth or a roaming attendant with a handheld capture system both work well in tighter interiors like a brownstone parlor floor, where a larger rig wouldn't.

faqs.q: Does the booth need special power?
faqs.a: Most booths need a standard 110V, 5-amp, 3-prong outlet within 15 feet, ideally not shared with the DJ or catering equipment. The 360 booth, vogue booth and Glambot need a dedicated 15 or 20-amp outlet instead, since they draw more power.

faqs.q: Can a photo booth be set up outdoors?
faqs.a: Yes, many of our booths can be set up outdoors when the site allows — a level, dry area with cover from rain and wind, plus the same outlet requirement as an indoor setup. We'll review your specific outdoor location with you before the day.

faqs.q: How long does setup take?
faqs.a: About 20 minutes for a standard booth once we're in the room. Larger installs like the vogue booth or Glambot can take closer to two hours at venues with restricted access, so we plan that into the schedule in advance.

faqs.q: What if I don't know my venue's exact dimensions?
faqs.a: That's normal — send us the venue name or a photo of the room and we'll tell you honestly which booth fits and whether anything about the space, like stairs or a shared electrical panel, needs planning around.

cta.heading: Not sure what your venue can fit?
cta.sub: Send us the room and we'll tell you honestly which booth works — and confirm power, access and setup time before you book.

meta.title: Photo Booth Insurance & COI Guide NYC | Magic Mirror Brooklyn
meta.description: What a certificate of insurance actually covers, why most NYC venues require one, and how fast we turn ours around from our $3 million policy.

h1: Certificates of Insurance for NYC Photo Booth Rentals
excerpt: If your venue has asked for a certificate of insurance and you're not sure what that means, here's the practical version — what's on our policy, what we need from you, and how fast it moves.

heroImg.alt: Photo booth activation at a corporate venue that required a certificate of insurance

body.heading: Why almost every NYC venue asks for one
paragraphs: If you've booked a wedding venue, a hotel ballroom or an office tower in New York, there's a good chance someone on the venue side has already asked your vendors for a certificate of insurance, or COI, before confirming load-in. It's not a formality specific to us — most venues require every outside vendor bringing equipment into the building to carry liability insurance and prove it in writing, usually naming the venue as an additional insured on the policy.

The logic is straightforward from the venue's side: if a piece of rented equipment damages the floor or a guest trips over a cable, the venue wants to know the vendor's insurer is on the hook, not the venue's own policy. It's routine, and it's rarely the thing that actually slows a booking down, as long as it's requested early enough.

The confusing part for a lot of couples and event planners booking their first vendor lineup is that nobody tells them this is coming until the venue mentions it in passing, sometimes weeks after the deposit is down. It's worth asking your venue coordinator directly, early, whether they require a COI from vendors — most do, and knowing the answer up front means it's one less thing to chase in the final weeks before your event.

body.heading: What's actually on our policy
paragraphs: We carry a $3 million general liability policy, which covers the range of standard requirements we see across wedding venues, hotels, office buildings and event spaces throughout NYC and the tri-state area. For the small number of venues that ask for a higher limit than that, or specific additional-insured wording, send us the exact requirement from your venue and we'll tell you directly whether we can meet it.

The policy is a fixed part of every booking, not an add-on — you're never asked to pay extra for the COI itself, and it applies whether you're booking a wedding, a corporate event or a multi-day trade show.

body.heading: Same-day turnaround, and why the timing matters
paragraphs: COI requests have a habit of landing late — a venue coordinator mentions it two weeks out, or a building's security desk asks for one the morning of load-in. Either way, we turn a certificate around the same day you send us the venue's name, address and the contact who needs to receive it, so a late request rarely becomes a scheduling problem.

For corporate accounts working to a purchase order or an opening account, the same document usually needs to satisfy both the venue's insurance requirement and your own vendor-onboarding paperwork — let us know both up front and we'll make sure the COI covers what each side actually needs.

body.heading: What we need from you to issue one
paragraphs: Four things move a COI request from ask to sent: the venue's legal name, its address, the contact email that should receive it, and any specific additional-insured wording the venue has given you. If you don't have that last part, forward us whatever the venue sent — we'll match the format they're expecting.
Reply to your booking confirmation with those details, or send them through the quote form if you're still deciding, and we'll issue the certificate the same day.

body.heading: Where this comes up most
paragraphs: Office towers and corporate venues are usually the strictest — a building engineer or security desk will often hold equipment at the loading dock until a COI naming the building is on file, so we build that step into every Downtown Brooklyn or Manhattan office booking as a matter of course, not a special request.

Trade shows add a second layer: many convention centers require a COI naming both the venue and the show's official decorator, since the decorator manages freight and load-in independently of the building itself. Send us the exhibitor kit and we'll handle our part of that paperwork alongside the venue's own requirement.

Weddings sit at the other end of the spectrum — most NYC reception venues ask for one, but it tends to be a single, straightforward request handled through the venue's own event coordinator rather than a multi-party building process. Either way, the certificate itself takes the same amount of time to issue on our end, so the venue type mostly changes who you're coordinating with, not how long you should expect to wait.

faqs.a: Yes. We carry a $3 million general liability policy that covers our events throughout NYC and the tri-state area.

faqs.q: How fast can you send a certificate of insurance?
faqs.a: Same day, once you send us the venue's name, address and the contact who needs to receive it. Most requests are turned around within hours.

faqs.q: Does the COI cost extra?
faqs.a: No. It's a standard part of every booking, not an add-on, whether it's for a wedding venue, a corporate office or a multi-day trade show.

faqs.q: What information do you need to issue one?
faqs.a: The venue's legal name and address, the contact email that should receive it, and any specific additional-insured wording the venue provided. Forward us whatever the venue sent if you're not sure of the exact wording.

faqs.q: Do trade show venues need anything different?
faqs.a: Often yes — many require a COI naming both the venue and the show's official decorator, since the decorator handles freight separately from the building. Send us the exhibitor kit and we'll cover both.

faqs.q: What if my venue asks for a higher policy limit than $3 million?
faqs.a: Send us the exact requirement and we'll tell you directly whether we can meet it — this comes up occasionally with larger corporate venues, and we'd rather confirm it early than after you've booked.

meta.title: Trade Show Photo Booth Checklist | Magic Mirror Brooklyn
meta.description: What we need before a trade show booking — exhibitor kit paperwork, load-in windows, multi-day staffing and lead capture — so your stand is ready on day one.

h1: Trade Show Photo Booth Checklist: What to Send Us First
excerpt: A trade show floor runs on a different clock than a wedding reception. Here's the exact list we work through before your show, so nothing holds up load-in.

heroImg.alt: Selfie photo booth drawing attendees to a trade show stand

body.heading: Why a trade show needs a different checklist
paragraphs: A wedding or a corporate party runs for one evening, in a room we can usually walk before the event. A trade show runs across a full show floor, over multiple days, on a schedule set by the venue and the show's general contractor rather than by us or by you. That means more of the planning has to happen before the show opens, and less of it can be figured out on the day.

None of this is a reason to overthink it — it just means a slightly different set of questions up front, most of which are already answered inside the paperwork your show organizer sends every exhibitor. The checklist below is the same one we work through with marketing teams and event agencies before every trade show booking, whether it's a first-time exhibitor or a company that runs a booth at a dozen shows a year.

body.heading: The exhibitor kit is the real checklist
paragraphs: Every trade show sends exhibitors a kit covering load-in windows, freight marshaling instructions, dock assignments and insurance requirements, and it's usually the fastest way for us to plan your booth's setup correctly. Send us the kit as soon as you have it and we'll pull out what applies to us: when we can bring equipment onto the floor, which dock or entrance to use, and what paperwork the show wants on file.

Insurance is the piece worth flagging early: many convention centers require a certificate of insurance naming both the venue and the show's official decorator, since the decorator manages freight independently of the building. We carry a $3 million policy and turn same-day COIs for both.

body.heading: Staffing across multiple show days
paragraphs: Multi-day bookings work differently from a single-evening rental. We set up before the floor opens on day one, staff your stand with a trained operator for every show day rather than a single shift, handle secure shutdown each night, and break down after the show closes — your own team never has to manage the equipment between sessions.

If your show runs mixed hours — an early setup day before doors, or a shortened final afternoon — tell us the exact show-day schedule from your exhibitor kit and we'll staff around it rather than a standard assumption.

body.heading: Turning stand traffic into a lead list
paragraphs: A booth's real job at a trade show is getting people to stop walking, and the second job is capturing something from them once they do. Attendees can opt in with an email address or phone number before receiving their photo, every image carries your branded overlay, and you get the full opt-in list alongside the gallery once the show ends — real contacts collected while someone was enjoying themselves, not dodging a badge scanner.
For teams that report on show ROI, we can break down sessions, shares and opt-ins by day, so the booth's line on the budget comes with numbers attached.

body.heading: Picking the right booth for a show floor
paragraphs: For a multi-day show with footfall spread evenly across the day rather than concentrated into one evening, a roaming photo booth usually earns more attention than a static one — an attendant works the aisle with a handheld capture system and brings the camera to people instead of waiting for a line to form. A branded booth, fully wrapped with your campaign graphics and a custom start screen, is the better call when the activation needs to look identical to the rest of your stand rather than sit apart from it.
Whichever booth fits your stand, it can be wrapped, overlaid and built around your brand end to end — nothing in the experience goes out generic.

body.heading: Getting your booking in early
paragraphs: Trade show floor space fills up fast, and so does our multi-day availability during peak convention season. A fully branded, multi-day booking benefits from two to three weeks' notice so wrap graphics can be printed and applied correctly, though digital-only branding can turn around faster if your show date is closer than that.
The earlier you send your exhibitor kit and show dates, the more of this checklist we can settle before your team is focused on the hundred other things a show floor demands that week.

faqs.q: What should I send you before our trade show?
faqs.a: Your exhibitor kit as soon as you have it — it covers load-in windows, freight marshaling and insurance requirements, which is usually all we need to plan your setup correctly.

faqs.q: Can the booth capture leads at our stand?
faqs.a: Yes — that's usually the point. Attendees opt in with an email address or phone number before receiving their photo, every capture carries your branded overlay, and you get the full opt-in list with the gallery after the show.

faqs.q: Do you handle exhibitor paperwork and insurance for the venue and the decorator?
faqs.a: Yes. Many convention centers require a certificate of insurance naming both the venue and the show's official decorator. We carry a $3 million policy and turn same-day COIs for both.

faqs.q: Can you staff a booth across a multi-day show?
faqs.a: Yes. Multi-day bookings include setup before opening, a trained operator on the stand for every show day, secure overnight shutdown, and breakdown after close.

faqs.q: Which booth works best for a trade show floor?
faqs.a: For footfall spread across a full day, the roaming photo booth usually covers more ground than a static one. For activations that need to match your stand's branding exactly, the fully branded booth is the better fit.

faqs.q: How much notice do you need for a trade show booking?
faqs.a: As much as you can give once your exhibitor kit is finalized — multi-day, fully branded activations benefit from two to three weeks' notice for wrap production, though we can move faster with digital-only branding if your show is closer than that.

h1: Photo Booth Rental Across Brooklyn's Neighborhoods
excerpt: Park Slope and Bushwick aren't the same planning problem, and neither are DUMBO and Bay Ridge. Here's how Brooklyn's neighborhoods actually differ for a photo booth setup, and where to find the guide for yours.

heroImg.alt: Guests using a photo booth at a celebration in Brooklyn

body.heading: Brooklyn isn't one planning problem
paragraphs: Say "Brooklyn" to most out-of-town vendors and they picture one borough with one set of logistics. We don't get that luxury — a Park Slope brownstone, a Bushwick freight-elevator loft, a Red Hook warehouse on the water and a Bay Ridge catering hall each come with a genuinely different setup, and we plan for the difference rather than showing up with a one-size answer.

This isn't a full directory — it's the pattern behind it, organized by the kind of venue each part of the borough tends to produce, with a pointer to the full local guide for wherever your event actually is. We keep a dedicated page for each neighborhood named below, with its own coverage area, FAQs and access notes.

body.heading: Brownstone Brooklyn: Park Slope and Crown Heights
paragraphs: Park Slope and Crown Heights share a housing stock more than a border — parlor floors, backyard tents and Prospect Park–adjacent venues built for showers, brunches and receptions under 100 guests, often in a private home rather than a rented hall. A narrow brownstone stairwell means the booth has to travel light, and a shared brownstone electrical panel gets confirmed ahead of time, not discovered on the day.

The compact mirror booth and the roaming booth both work well on a parlor floor or in a tented yard where floor space is limited. Our Park Slope and Crown Heights guides go deeper on both neighborhoods, including which venues we've already worked in.

body.heading: Industrial lofts: Williamsburg, Bushwick and Gowanus
paragraphs: These three neighborhoods share the same building stock — converted warehouses and manufacturing floors with the ceiling height that lets the 360 booth's camera arm complete a full orbit and the vogue booth's LED backdrop actually read. They also share the same access variable: freight elevators that run on their own schedule, some stopping by early evening, which is why we confirm freight hours with the venue before the day rather than assuming they'll be running when guests arrive.

Gowanus sits between Park Slope and Red Hook geographically and shares Bushwick's loft-conversion logistics, which makes it a convenient middle ground for guests coming from either direction. Our Williamsburg, Bushwick and Gowanus guides each break down the specific buildings and streets we're out on most weekends.

body.heading: Waterfront Brooklyn: DUMBO, Greenpoint and Red Hook
paragraphs: Waterfront venues photograph beautifully and plan differently. DUMBO's cobblestone streets mean load-in gets scheduled block by block; Greenpoint's West Street venues share Williamsburg's rooftop-and-pier planning realities, including a wind and weather plan for outdoor power; and Red Hook is the one neighborhood on this list with no direct subway access, so we build extra travel and load-in time into every quote there rather than treating it like a five-minute-away run.

Once we're on site, the water and industrial backdrop across all three needs almost no dressing up — the 360 booth and green screen booth both do well in the open floor plans these buildings tend to have. Our DUMBO, Greenpoint and Red Hook guides cover the specific access notes for each.

body.heading: Corporate and catering-hall Brooklyn: Downtown Brooklyn and Bay Ridge
paragraphs: Downtown Brooklyn is the borough's corporate core — office towers around MetroTech, hotel ballrooms, and a growing cluster of companies near Barclays Center — where a loading dock, a security check-in and a building engineer asking for a certificate of insurance are standard, not special requests. Bay Ridge runs on a different model entirely: catering halls along 3rd and 5th Avenues that book an entire evening around one wedding, sweet sixteen or engagement party, often for 150 guests or more, with an in-house coordinator we work directly with on timing.

Both neighborhoods can comfortably support a bigger footprint than brownstone or loft Brooklyn — a full 360 booth orbit or a red-carpet mirror setup has the room it needs in either. Our Downtown Brooklyn and Bay Ridge guides go deeper on both.

faqs.q: Do you serve every neighborhood in Brooklyn?
faqs.a: Yes. Beyond the neighborhoods covered here, we're out across the whole borough most weekends — if your venue isn't listed on one of our neighborhood guides, ask anyway and we'll tell you honestly whether we can get there.

faqs.q: Does the neighborhood affect the price?
faqs.a: Most of Brooklyn carries no travel fee since we're based here — it's quoted from your venue's ZIP code before you book either way, so it's part of your upfront number rather than a surprise later.

faqs.q: Which Brooklyn neighborhoods need extra load-in planning?
faqs.a: Loft neighborhoods like Bushwick, Williamsburg and Gowanus often involve freight elevators with their own schedules, and Red Hook has no direct subway access, so we build extra time into quotes for all four. We'll flag it upfront if your venue needs it.

faqs.q: Can the same booth work in a brownstone and a warehouse?
faqs.a: Not always the same one. A brownstone parlor floor usually calls for a compact mirror or roaming setup, while a warehouse loft has the ceiling height for the 360 or vogue booth. Tell us your venue and we'll recommend the right fit.

faqs.q: How do I find the guide for my specific neighborhood?
faqs.a: Search our site for "photo booth rental" plus your neighborhood name, or just send us your venue on the quote form — we'll confirm coverage and pricing directly.
